notes: Turkish Kurd asylum return-risk appeal; Sedley LJ remitted for IAT to address airport interrogation concerns.

enrichment.short_title: Degirmenci: remittal on risk to returned Kurdish asylum-seekers at Ankara airport
key_facts: Alevi Kurd appellant entered the UK illegally in July 2002 and claimed asylum, alleging repeated army detention and ill-treatment in Turkey linked to PKK and HADEP associations.
The adjudicator and IAT found he could internally relocate to Ankara and faced no real risk on return because he would not be suspected at the airport.
HADEP, for which he had distributed leaflets, was banned by the Constitutional Court in March 2003 as aiding the PKK.
CIPU reports indicated returned asylum-seekers suspected of PKK links could be handed to the anti-terror branch where torture could not be ruled out.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal with permission granted by Dyson LJ after the IAT dismissed the asylum and human rights appeal and refused further permission.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to a differently constituted IAT with directions from the President, because the IAT had not adequately addressed whether return risk at Ankara airport vitiated internal relocation.
enrichment.ratio: If there is a real risk of detention and ill-treatment on arrival at the airport, internal relocation to Ankara is not a realistic option; the IAT must address unanswered questions about records of prior detentions, HADEP links and treatment of returned Kurdish asylum-seekers.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator applied too high a standard of proof to past ill-treatment findings
Whether risk on return at Ankara airport was properly assessed
Whether internal relocation remained viable if airport detention risk existed
Whether fresh country evidence introduced on appeal should be considered
linked_authorities: Sivakumaran v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1988] IMM AR 147
Suleyman Okur (IAT, 26 February 2000)
Karanakaran v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2000] 3 All ER 449

confidence.notes: Remittal reasoning and central airport-risk logic are clearly articulated by Sedley LJ.

notes: Restrictive covenant mandatory demolition appeal; delay in seeking interim relief held not to bar final injunction.

enrichment.short_title: Mortimer v Bailey: mandatory injunction despite delay over light covenant breach
key_facts: Neighbours at The Heugh and The Old Barn were bound by a 1992 covenant requiring written approval before building, not to be unreasonably withheld.
Defendants built a rear extension without consent after planning permission was granted, despite claimants' objections about loss of light, winter sunlight and view.
Claimants did not seek an interim injunction until late July 2003, after work had substantially progressed; Judge Armstrong refused interim relief on damages adequacy and delay grounds.
Trial judge found refusal of consent reasonable, assessed diminution in value at £20,000 and ordered demolition by mandatory injunction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on permission limited to whether delay in seeking an interim injunction should have barred a final mandatory injunction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge was entitled to grant mandatory demolition requiring restoration of the status quo ante.
enrichment.ratio: Delay in seeking an interim injunction is a relevant discretionary factor but does not generally debar a final mandatory injunction where the claimant promptly warned of proceedings, never indicated willingness to accept damages, and the defendant knowingly gambled on proceeding in breach of covenant.
legal_issues: Whether claimants' delay amounted to standing by or acquiescence
Whether Gafford v Graham required refusal of mandatory relief
Whether Shelfer damages in lieu principles applied
Whether damages were an adequate remedy for loss of covenant protection
linked_authorities: Gafford v Graham [1999] 3 EGLR 75
Shelfer v City of London Electric Lighting Co Ltd [1895] 1 Ch 287
Jaggard v Sawyer [1995] 1 WLR 269

confidence.notes: Single ground of appeal and discretionary analysis are detailed and conclusive.

notes: Open Spaces Society challenge to s.194 common land fencing consent; Collins J upheld longstanding DEFRA construction.

enrichment.short_title: Ashbrook v DEFRA: s.194 common land fencing consent and public local inquiry
key_facts: The Open Spaces Society challenged the Secretary of State's consent under section 194 to stock fencing on Wisley Common, an SSSI heathland in Surrey.
Surrey County Council sought fencing to enable low-intensity grazing to preserve heathland and prevent stock straying onto busy roads.
The OSS did not oppose grazing but objected to fencing as contrary to public enjoyment of common land.
DEFRA had for decades approved section 194 applications without a public local inquiry in most cases, using published criteria for when an inquiry was needed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim for a declaration that section 194 required a public local inquiry and an order quashing the fencing consent.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; section 194 did not require a public local inquiry in every approvable case, and the words 'if necessary hold the same inquiries' permitted the defendant's longstanding construction.
enrichment.ratio: Section 194(1) requires the Minister to hold the same inquiries as under the Commons Act 1876 only if necessary; that does not mandate a public local inquiry for every prima facie allowable application, and the plural 'inquiries' may refer generically to the local inquiry procedure in section 10(6).
legal_issues: Whether section 194 requires a public local inquiry before every consent
Construction of 'if necessary hold the same inquiries'
Effect of section 10(6) of the Commons Act 1876
Whether Pepper v Hart material from 1893 or 1925 assisted construction
linked_authorities: Pepper v Hart [1993] AC 593

confidence.notes: Statutory construction issue and dismissal are clearly reasoned, though the claim raised no merits challenge.

notes: Drink-driving case stated on completion of s.8(2) breath replacement option; Forbes J upheld unequivocal refusal.

enrichment.short_title: Ijaz v DPP: when the section 8(2) breath replacement option is completed
key_facts: Appellant was stopped in Luton in July 2003 and provided two breath specimens of 49 and a higher reading micrograms per 100 millilitres.
Because the lower reading was no more than 50, section 8(2) entitled him to claim replacement by blood or urine; PC Watkins read the option and recorded his answer as 'No'.
Two to three minutes after the procedure completed at 4.11am, the appellant said he had not wanted blood because of a needle phobia.
Magistrates convicted him, finding the option procedure properly completed and the breath specimen reliable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Luton Magistrates' Court to the High Court on when the section 7(3) and 8(2) replacement procedure is completed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the question was answered in the affirmative that the procedure was properly completed when the appellant gave an unequivocal 'No'.
enrichment.ratio: Where a driver is given a comprehensible section 8(2) option and gives an unequivocal refusal, the procedure is completed when that answer is entered; a later partial explanation for refusing blood is not a purported exercise of the statutory option nor a case of inability to make up one's mind.
legal_issues: When the section 8(2) replacement procedure is completed
Whether the appellant's later phobia explanation revived the option
Application of Smith v DPP on indecision versus unequivocal refusal
Whether police should have allowed further reflection time
linked_authorities: Smith v Director of Public Prosecutions [1989] RTR 159

confidence.notes: Facts found by magistrates and Forbes J's affirmative answer are straightforward.

notes: Masked shotgun murder appeal; Court of Appeal upheld Turnbull treatment of limited visual and voice recognition.

enrichment.short_title: Davies v R: Turnbull recognition evidence through Scream mask and voice
key_facts: Andrew Davies was convicted by a 10-1 jury majority of murdering Andrew Lansdown and causing GBH with intent to Steven Wemyss during a masked shotgun attack at Killingworth.
Surviving victim Steven Wemyss claimed to recognise Davies by eyes visible through a Scream mask and by voice asking 'Where's Chrissie?'.
There was extensive background animosity between Davies and the Wemyss/Lansdown families, including a visit to the house two hours before the shootings.
Trial counsel did not object to admission of the recognition evidence; co-accused Powell was acquitted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeal on leave as to whether trial counsel should have excluded recognition evidence, with additional summing-up grounds considered as if leave granted.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; trial counsel's conduct was not inexplicable and the judge's Turnbull directions were correct, with substantial circumstantial evidence capable of supporting the recognitions.
enrichment.ratio: Purported recognition of familiar eyes and voice during an incident is not an exceptional case for pre-trial exclusion under Turnbull; even weak identification may support conviction where other evidence makes the jury sure, and counsel may reasonably leave procedural criticisms to summing-up.
legal_issues: Whether visual and voice recognition evidence should have been excluded before trial
Whether the judge should have withdrawn the case or directed the evidence worthless
Construction of Turnbull where identification evidence is poor but supported by other evidence
Whether trial counsel acted contrary to reason and good sense
linked_authorities: R v Turnbull [1977] QB 224
R v Flemming (1986) 86 Cr App R 33
Hersey [1997] EWCA Crim 3106

confidence.notes: Long judgment but the dispositive Turnbull and ineffective-assistance analysis is explicit.

notes: Section 288 gypsy site planning challenge; Sullivan J rejected nine grounds and refused permission to appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Smith v SoS: gypsy caravan site retention refused at Woodside Hatch
key_facts: Claimant sought to retain four family plots with 12 caravans at Woodside Caravan Park, Hatch, Bedfordshire, after years of unauthorised occupation and enforcement history.
Northern field plots had been cleared following a High Court injunction; the appeal concerned the southern field only.
Inspector dismissed the appeal citing countryside harm, residential amenity, fear of crime, flood risk, policy undermining and concentration of gypsy sites near Sandy.
Residents feared recurrence of past crime and nuisance associated with earlier large-scale encampments, though recent incidents had decreased.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application under section 288 to quash an inspector's decision dismissing a planning appeal to retain a gypsy caravan site.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on all nine grounds; permission to appeal refused as hopeless.
enrichment.ratio: Fear of crime may be a material planning consideration even without proof that current occupiers committed offences; unauthorised establishment of a site and risk of reoccupation of adjoining land may legitimately weigh against retention where planning permission would run with the land.
legal_issues: Whether residents' fear of crime was a justified material consideration
Whether inspector erred in considering commercial greyhound training amenity loss
Whether risk of reoccupation of the northern field was relevant
Whether prior unlawful occupation could be considered on the merits
linked_authorities: West Midlands Probation Committee v Secretary of State for the Environment [1997] JPL 323
Newport Borough Council v Secretary of State for Wales [1998] Env LR 174
South Buckinghamshire District Council v Porter (No 2) [2004] UKHL 33

confidence.notes: Nine grounds are addressed systematically though the judgment is long and selective on extracts.

notes: TCC enforcement of second DOM/2 adjudication on extension of time; prior bedroom adjudication did not oust jurisdiction.

enrichment.short_title: Emcor Drake v Costain Skanska: enforcing second DOM/2 extension-of-time adjudication
key_facts: EDS sub-contracted electrical services at the Great Western Royal Hotel Paddington refurbishment under DOM/2 1981.
CSJV breached clause 11.7 by failing within 16 weeks of practical completion to extend, shorten or confirm the completion date.
Miller adjudication on the November 2002 bedroom delay claim held EDS had not proved entitlement to extension to 30 November 2001.
Hough adjudication on the February 2004 claim awarded extension to 25 February 2002 and £201,069.34 plus VAT, accepting bedroom slippage was non-critical.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court application to enforce Mr Hough's adjudication decision against jurisdictional and abuse-of-process challenges.
enrichment.outcome: Adjudicator Hough's decision enforced; he had jurisdiction and did not exceed it by reconsidering matters bound by Miller only to the extent permitted.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 11.7 does not permit only one extension-of-time adjudication; a later adjudicator may decide a broader claim where the earlier decision addressed only bedroom delays and did not confirm the previous completion date or finally dispose of all entitlement under clause 11.7.
legal_issues: Whether Miller's decision finally determined all extension-of-time entitlement
Whether Hough exceeded jurisdiction by reconsidering bedroom-related facts
Whether resubmitting prior documentation in a second adjudication was an abuse of process
Whether CSJV could grant only one extension under clause 11.7

confidence.notes: Interlocutory enforcement reasoning is clear though some DOM/2 clause detail remains contextual.

notes: Case stated on meaning of 'breath' in drink-driving law; Silber J held it includes all exhaled air.

enrichment.short_title: Zafar v DPP: 'breath' in section 5 RTA includes mouth alcohol
key_facts: Appellant, a medical doctor, was convicted after Intoximeter readings of 79 and 75 micrograms when the limit was 35.
He claimed heartburn/reflux could produce mouth alcohol and that section 5 required proof of alcohol in deep lung air only.
Professor Makin gave evidence that Intoximeters are designed to detect deep lung air but are often unreliable at excluding mouth alcohol.
The Crown Court rejected the deep-lung-only construction and dismissed the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated on the meaning of 'breath' in section 5 RTA and section 15(2) RTOA.
enrichment.outcome: Question answered 'no' to confining 'breath' to deep lung air; appeal dismissed and late application to amend the case stated refused.
enrichment.ratio: In the absence of contrary statutory intention, 'breath' in section 5(1)(a) bears its ordinary meaning of all exhaled air and is not limited to deep lung air; Parliament did not distinguish mouth alcohol, and later ministerial statements on Intoximeter design do not construe the 1988 Act.
legal_issues: Whether 'breath' means deep lung air only or all exhaled air
Relevance of Intoximeter design and Home Office approval
Whether Pepper v Hart debates on later RTA amendments assisted construction
Whether the Crown Court should have directed acquittal for mouth alcohol
linked_authorities: Webber v Cary [1970] AC 1072
Pepper v Hart [1993] AC 593
DPP v Texeira [2003] RTR 395

confidence.notes: Single statutory construction question answered directly with clear reasoning.

notes: Prison disciplinary JR over urine test refusal; Wilson J quashed finding for disclosure and witness failures.

enrichment.short_title: Szuluk: prison adjudication quashed for unfair disclosure and witness handling
key_facts: Serving prisoner at HMP Full Sutton refused a lawful order to provide a urine sample for mandatory drug testing, citing solicitor advice.
Reasonable suspicion depended on warder Harrison's account of smelling burning and seeing foil heating in the claimant's cell the previous evening.
The adjudicator directed disclosure of documents relating to reasonable suspicion on 11 July 2003, but on 27 August was misled into believing no such direction had been made.
Mr Alexander, a cellmate the claimant wished to call, was wrongly said to be unavailable and never asked to attend.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's refusal to quash an independent adjudicator's finding of guilt and imposed privilege forfeitures.
enrichment.outcome: Secretary of State's decision quashed; mandatory order requiring quashing of the adjudicator's finding because the hearing was unfair.
enrichment.ratio: A prison disciplinary hearing must be fair at common law; it was unfair to proceed after the adjudicator was misled about a disclosure direction and after a requested witness was incorrectly treated as unavailable when he was willing and able to attend.
legal_issues: Whether failure to disclose Harrison's statement before the hearing invalidated the adjudication
Whether the adjudicator was misled about his earlier disclosure direction
Whether denial of Mr Alexander's attendance was unfair
Whether reasonable suspicion existed on the facts ultimately before the adjudicator
linked_authorities: R v Blundeston Prison Board of Visitors, ex parte Fox-Taylor [1982] 1 All ER 646
R (Napier) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWHC Admin 936

confidence.notes: Two distinct fairness grounds and remedial orders are clearly explained.

notes: ERA reinstatement compensation appeal; section 114(2)(a) arrears caught by statutory cap per Selfridges.

enrichment.short_title: NatWest v Parry: section 114(2)(a) arrears subject to compensatory award cap
key_facts: Mr Parry, a 33-year NatWest branch manager, was unfairly dismissed and the tribunal ordered reinstatement despite the bank stating it would not comply.
Total compensation of £94,583.72 comprised basic award, capped compensatory award, additional award under section 117(3)(b), and £21,188.72 arrears under section 114(2)(a).
The bank did not reinstate; the employee's wider loss appeal failed because of the statutory cap.
The bank cross-appealed that the section 114(2)(a) arrears should also be subject to the section 124 cap.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal on permission limited to whether arrears specified under section 114(2)(a) are ring-fenced from the section 124 compensatory award cap.
enrichment.outcome: Employee's appeal dismissed; section 114(2)(a) arrears form part of the section 117(3)(a) compensatory award and are subject to the statutory cap except to the limited extent provided in section 124(4).
enrichment.ratio: An amount specified under section 114(2)(a) is payable on compliance with a reinstatement order; if the order is not complied with, that sum forms part of the compensatory award under section 117(3)(a) and is caught by section 124 unless section 124(4) permits the cap to be exceeded to reflect arrears net of the additional award.
legal_issues: Whether section 114(2)(a) arrears are free-standing or part of the compensatory award
Construction of section 124(4) and its interaction with section 117(3)
Whether Selfridges Ltd v Malek was correctly applied
Effect of a reinstatement order where the employer refuses compliance
linked_authorities: Selfridges Ltd v Malek [1998] ICR 268
O'Laoire v Jackel International Ltd [1990] ICR 197
Midland Mainline v CM Wade, 4 November 2002 (unreported)
